title: Poverty and zakat today
hook: a blanket, a bowl and an axe: giving that lifts

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hijra today: a cave, a welcome in Medina, and a man asking the way to the market. What did you give, or whose name did you learn? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

A man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asking for help. The story is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. The Prophet asks him: is there nothing in your house? There is: a blanket, and a bowl for drinking water. The Prophet takes them, sells them to the people sitting nearby, and hands the man the money with instructions. Buy food for your family with part of it. With the rest, buy an axe head, and bring it to me. The Prophet fixes a handle to it himself and sends the man out to gather wood and sell it. Today: giving that feeds, and giving that lifts.
screen: `A BLANKET AND A BOWL.` → `AN AXE HEAD, A HANDLE.` → `GIVING THAT LIFTS.`

segments.voice: Zakat, the obligatory alms, is counted among the pillars of Islam: a share of wealth, given by those who have enough, to those the Qur'an names. The list is in surah nine. In Pickthall's translation it begins: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy," and it goes on to name those who collect the alms, those whose hearts are to be won, captives to be freed, people in debt, the cause of Allah, and the traveler. Notice how many of those are about getting someone out of something: out of chains, out of debt, out of being stranded. A few verses later the Qur'an says to the Prophet: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Purify and grow. In al-Bukhari, when the Prophet sends Mu'adh to Yemen, he tells him to teach the people that zakat is taken from their rich and returned to their poor. Taken from here, given back there, in the same place. So what does zakat look like today? It is still calculated on savings, gold and business stock, and given through mosques, through charities and by hand. Some zakat funds pay off debts, or pay for a sick person's care, or help a family start a small trade. Scholars discuss which uses fit the categories in the verse, and some debate whether zakat can fund long-term projects or should go straight to people. Behind the debate is the axe in the hook. The hope behind zakat is more than a meal. It's the moment someone no longer needs to ask.
screen: `A PILLAR: A SHARE OF WEALTH.` · `THE ALMS ARE ONLY FOR THE POOR.` · `PURIFY THEM AND MAKE THEM GROW.` · `FROM THEIR RICH, TO THEIR POOR.` · then, large: `SO THAT NO ONE NEEDS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The practice: give with thought. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person or one place you've given to before, or meant to. Picture what happened to the gift after it left your hands. Did it feed someone for a day? Did it clear a debt, or buy a tool, or pay a fee that let someone keep working? Don't grade yourself. Just look. Then picture one gift you could give this month, of any size, and ask the axe question: could this help someone stand up, as well as eat? If you pray, you can ask for a giving that purifies and grows. The bell holds the time.
Poverty and zakat today. The share of wealth the Qur'an assigns to the poor, the indebted and the stranded, and the hope that it lifts people, not just feeds them. Today's word.
Your line: zakat can lift. Today, before you give anything, ask what it will do after it leaves your hands. Tomorrow, scholarship today. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims who have enough wealth calculate their zakat each year and give it through mosques, zakat funds, charities or directly to people in need who fall within the Qur'an's categories.

fork.setup: a man comes asking for help. he owns a blanket and a drinking bowl. you're the Prophet. what do you do?
options: give him a meal and send him home.
sell his things, and send him off with food money and an axe.

original.note: Arabic: the obligatory alms given each year from wealth.

trapdoor: what you thought: zakat is a charity tax.
what it means: a share of wealth the Qur'an assigns by name to the poor, the indebted, captives and travelers, meant to lift as well as feed.
what a scholar hears: 9:60's named recipients, 9:103's alms that purify them and make them grow, and Mu'adh sent to Yemen: taken from their rich, returned to their poor.

Confirm Abu Dawud 1641 and its grading; the story is retold here as the hook (blanket, bowl, axe head, handle). The ending (the man later returns having earned, and the teaching on begging) is left out.
Confirm Pickthall's exact wording of 9:60 (opening) and 9:103. The 9:60 categories are paraphrased; 'those whose hearts are to be won' paraphrases Pickthall's 'whose hearts are to be reconciled'.
'One of the pillars of Islam' and 'calculate it on savings, gold, business stock' describe standard practice without figures (no nisab or percentage given); confirm.
